templates.name: Blank completion, phrase options (word + preposition, a/an + word)
Blank completion, contrast clue (including received view then finding)
Blank completion, cause or consequence clue
Most nearly mean, underlined phrase or phrase options

items.passage: Reflective fleece covers spread across portions of Swiss glaciers each summer reduce melting beneath them by roughly 60 percent, protecting ski-run ice ramps and a tourist grotto inside the Rhône Glacier. Because covering every Swiss glacier would nonetheless cost over a billion francs annually and merely slow the decline, Matthias Huss and colleagues regard the covers as ______ glacier retreat.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A palliative eases a problem where it is felt without removing its cause. The covers work locally (about 60 percent less melting, a ski ramp and a grotto saved), but covering every glacier would be far too costly and would still only slow the decline. So Huss and colleagues see the covers as relief for particular patches of ice, not a remedy for retreat itself.

A.why_wrong: A panacea is a cure for everything. The text says covering all the glaciers would cost over a billion francs a year and would still only slow their decline, so the covers are far from a cure.

B.why_wrong: A harbinger is a sign that something is coming. The covers respond to retreat that is already happening; nothing presents them as a warning of it.

D.why_wrong: A catalyst speeds a process up. The covers reduce melting under them, so they slow retreat rather than hasten it.

band7_moves: clue is the consequence only: local success plus prohibitive scale implies relief without cure
option set past rank 10,000 except one reversal

sources.what: WSL press release on Huss et al., Cold Regions Science and Technology: about 60% less melt under the white tarpaulins; used on ski areas (Gemsstock) and the Rhône Glacier ice grotto; covering all Swiss glaciers would cost over CHF 1 billion a year and only slow the decline; not a silver bullet

items.notes: Subject: natural science (glaciology). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (covers work locally but cannot be scaled and only slow the loss, so they relieve without curing; then match that to the medical figure). Concessive frame: yes (effective, but). Transferred-sense key: yes (palliative, a medical word used of a policy). Corrected ranks (reviewer recount, measure calibrated to the band-7 report): a panacea for 27,745; a harbinger of 32,004; a palliative for 39,851; a catalyst for 5,487; 3 of 4 past 10,000; mean log 4.32. Band-5 guard: clear (key not the only rare option). Near miss: panacea (right field, wrong degree).

band7.why: 3 of 4 options past rank 10,000 (only catalyst, 5,487, is common), mean log 4.32; key palliative (39,851) in a transferred medical sense; the clue is the consequence only (works locally, unaffordable at scale, merely slows the loss); panacea is a near miss on degree. Rarest distractor 32,004 misses check 2, checks 1 and 3 pass.

items.passage: In a field experiment in Uttar Pradesh, India, economist Matt Lowe randomly assigned young men to cricket teams and opponents. Participants whose teammates belonged to other castes subsequently formed more cross-caste friendships, whereas those who merely competed against other castes formed fewer. Whether intercaste contact alleviated or intensified divisions was thus ______ the form that contact took.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To be contingent on something is to depend on it. Playing with men of other castes led to more cross-caste friendships, while playing against them led to fewer, so whether contact helped or hurt depended on the form of contact.

B.why_wrong: Extraneous to means unrelated to. The two forms of contact had opposite effects, so the form of contact was central to the outcome, not unrelated to it.

C.why_wrong: Proportional to describes an amount that grows with another amount. The text contrasts two kinds of contact with opposite effects; it does not say that more of something produced more of the effect, and a form of contact is not a quantity.

D.why_wrong: Antithetical to means directly opposed to. Nothing suggests that the outcome of contact opposed the form of contact; the text shows that the outcome depended on it.

band7_moves: the consequence is the only clue (opposite outcomes imply dependence)
near-miss distractor naming the wrong kind of dependence (proportional to)
three of four options past rank 10,000, rarest distractor unseen (antithetical to)

sources.what: AEA Research Highlight on Lowe, “Types of Contact” (American Economic Review 2021): randomized cricket leagues in rural Uttar Pradesh; other-caste teammates increased other-caste friendships, other-caste opponents decreased them

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics). Key letter A. Steps: 2 (two forms of contact gave opposite results, so the result depended on the form; then pick the word for dependence). Concessive frame: no. Transferred-sense key: no. Corrected ranks (reviewer recount, measure calibrated to the band-7 report): contingent on 17,762; extraneous to 27,907; proportional to 7,434; antithetical to unseen; 3 of 4 past 10,000; mean log 4.64. Near miss: proportional to (a dependence, but of amount on amount).

band7.why: 3 of 4 options past 10,000 (proportional to 7,434), mean log 4.64, rarest distractor antithetical to unseen; academic word + preposition key as in mediated by; two steps (opposite outcomes imply dependence) with a near miss on the kind of dependence. The Whether ... or frame points to dependence plainly, so the vocabulary carries the item.

fixes: notes and band7_moves said all four options past rank 10,000; proportional to is 7,434 (3 of 4, mean log 4.64)

items.passage: Fred Wilson’s 1992 installation Mining the Museum used objects that the Maryland Historical Society owned but seldom displayed to expose what its exhibitions had long ______. In a case of ornate silver vessels, Wilson placed iron slave shackles, and beside a row of busts he installed empty pedestals inscribed with the names of Harriet Tubman, Benjamin Banneker, and Frederick Douglass.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To elide something is to leave it out or pass over it in silence. The installation used objects the society owned but seldom displayed, and the empty pedestals stand for people its exhibitions had left out. What Wilson exposed, then, is what the exhibitions had long omitted.

A.why_wrong: To foreground something is to give it prominence. The text says the society seldom displayed the objects Wilson used, so its exhibitions had not given them prominence.

B.why_wrong: Fabricated means invented or faked. Wilson used objects from the society’s own collection, and nothing suggests the displays had made anything up.

C.why_wrong: Repatriated means returned to a country of origin, a word from museum practice. Nothing in the text concerns returning objects; the installation is about what the displays left out.

band7_moves: rare key (elided) with equally rare distractors
clue given only by examples of absence, in a different register from the key

sources.what: Beautiful Trouble, Mining the Museum: Wilson re-contextualized the Maryland Historical Society’s collection; Metalwork 1793–1880 case with iron slave shackles among ornate silver pitchers and goblets; empty pedestals named for Harriet Tubman, Benjamin Banneker and Frederick Douglass; “what they don’t put on view says even more”

items.notes: Subject: humanities (art, museums). Key letter D. Steps: 2 (objects seldom displayed and empty pedestals show what was left out; then the rare word for leaving out). Clue register differs from the key: plain, concrete wording (seldom displayed, empty pedestals) for a Latinate key. “Seldom displayed” rests on Wilson’s own line in the source. Corrected ranks: foregrounded 13,287; fabricated 48,264; repatriated unseen; elided unseen; 4 of 4 past 10,000; mean log 5.20. Band-5 guard: clear (distractors as rare as the key). Detail simplified: the busts (Clay, Napoleon, Jackson) are not named.

band7.why: 4 of 4 options past 10,000, mean log 5.20 (elided and repatriated unseen, fabricated 48,264); band-5 guard clear since the distractors are as rare as the key; the clue comes only as concrete examples of absence in a plain register, and expose ... fabricated is a natural collocation trap.

items.passage: Carved on standing stones in early medieval Scotland, Pictish symbols have often been interpreted as ______ devices: like the insignia on a coat of arms, each would have identified a family or a rank. When Rob Lee and colleagues measured how predictably one symbol follows another, however, the sequences more closely resembled those of written languages.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The blank describes the older interpretation, which the text compares to the insignia on a coat of arms identifying a family or rank. Symbols that stand for an identity in that way are emblematic. Lee’s finding is then set against this view with “however”: the sequences look like writing instead.

A.why_wrong: Phonetic symbols represent speech sounds, which is closer to the writing-like pattern Lee’s team found. The blank describes the earlier view that “however” contrasts with that finding.

C.why_wrong: Votive objects are offered in fulfillment of a vow, often in a sacred place. The text says the symbols were thought to mark a family or rank, not to serve as offerings.

D.why_wrong: Calendrical symbols would record dates or seasons. Nothing in the text connects the symbols to time; the older view treats them as markers of family or rank.

sources.what: Lee, Jonathan and Ziman 2010, Proceedings of the Royal Society A: Shannon-entropy analysis of Pictish symbol sequences finds them unlikely to be random or heraldic and showing characteristics of written languages

items.notes: Subject: social science (archaeology, linguistics). Key letter B. Received view then finding, with the blank on the view being challenged and the finding’s trait (phonetic) offered as the reversal. Band 6 target (B3 assignment). Corrected ranks: phonetic 48,763; emblematic 28,969; votive 34,866; calendrical unseen. Hedged as in the source: “more closely resembled” written languages, not “are writing.”

band7.why: By the measure: 4 of 4 options past 20,000, mean log 4.92, calendrical unseen; B3 received view then finding with the blank on the view and the finding's trait (phonetic) as the reversal. Caveat: one step, the coat-of-arms simile restates the key, and emblematic and calendrical are transparent from emblem and calendar, so it plays easier than its ranks. band_target was 6. Lead (2026-10-20): kept at band 6, its band_target; the reviewer found it plays easier than its ranks (one step, guessable words).

items.passage: Because morning sunshine conveys no information about companies’ future earnings, economists who assume that stock prices respond exclusively to such information would expect the weather to be ______ to daily market returns. Nevertheless, analyzing exchanges in 26 countries, David Hirshleifer and Tyler Shumway found that sunnier mornings in an exchange’s home city were associated with higher returns.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: If prices respond only to news about earnings, and sunshine carries no such news, then the weather should make no difference to returns: it should be immaterial to them. The “Nevertheless” sentence then reports the surprise, that sunny mornings went with higher returns.

A.why_wrong: Germane means relevant. Economists who think prices respond only to earnings news, which sunshine does not carry, would expect the weather to be irrelevant to returns, not relevant to them.

B.why_wrong: Detrimental means harmful. Nothing in the economists’ assumption gives a reason to expect sunshine to hurt returns; it gives a reason to expect no effect.

C.why_wrong: Analogous means similar in some way. The economists’ reasoning concerns whether weather affects returns, not whether the two resemble each other.

band7_moves: received view then finding, with the blank on the view and the key implied by a negated premise (carries no information)
key in its secondary sense (immaterial as irrelevant, not bodiless)
three of four options past rank 10,000, rarest distractor germane 57,248
reversal of the implied logic (germane) rather than of a stated word

sources.what: Hirshleifer and Shumway, “Good Day Sunshine: Stock Returns and the Weather” (Journal of Finance 2003): morning sunshine at the city of a country’s leading exchange is strongly correlated with daily index returns in 26 countries, 1982–1997; hard to reconcile with fully rational price setting
Ohio State University news release on Hirshleifer and Shumway: sunshine at 26 major stock exchanges linked to same-day market returns, 1982 to 1997

items.notes: Subject: social science (finance). Key letter D. Negation sits in “carries no news” in the blank’s sentence, and the key is the conclusion that negated fact implies (no news, so no effect), the band-7 B5 move of d3ca5d59. Steps: 2. Corrected ranks (reviewer recount, measure calibrated to the band-7 report): germane 57,248; detrimental 28,955; analogous 4,374; immaterial 24,726; 3 of 4 past 10,000; mean log 4.31. No negation-flip distractor.

band7.why: After the fix: 3 of 4 options past 10,000, mean log 4.31, rarest distractor germane 57,248; key immaterial in its secondary sense (irrelevant); received view then finding with the blank on the view, two steps. Before the fix it was 2 of 4, mean log 4.06, a band-6 option set.

fixes: replaced integral (corrected rank 5,487) with germane (57,248): the notes put integral and analogous past 10,000 but both are under it, so the set read band 6 (2 of 4, mean log 4.06); now 3 of 4, mean log 4.31, rarest distractor past 50,000
rewrote distractor A and the notes and band7_moves to match
added a working source URL (the econwpa PDF refused connection)

items.subtype: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
items.passage: Greek, unlike English, has separate basic terms for light blue (ghalazio) and dark blue (ble). Because of this lexical distinction, the contrast between the two shades may be more ______ to Greek speakers: in experiments by Guillaume Thierry and colleagues, Greek speakers’ neural responses registered a shift from one blue to the other more strongly than English speakers’ responses did.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Salient means standing out, easily noticed. The cause is in the “Because” clause: Greek names the two blues separately. The study then shows Greek speakers’ brains reacting more strongly to a change between them, so the difference stands out more for them.

B.why_wrong: Inscrutable means impossible to make out. Greek speakers’ brains registered the shift more strongly, so the difference is easier for them to notice, not harder.

C.why_wrong: Ostentatious means showy, displayed to impress. It belongs to things or people that call attention to themselves on purpose; a difference between shades does not show off, it is simply noticed more.

D.why_wrong: Innate means inborn. The text traces the effect to the Greek language’s two words, something speakers learn, not to anything they are born with.

band7_moves: cause in a Because clause, evaluative key
near-miss distractor on agent and intent (ostentatious)
reversal of the cause (innate) as a second trap

sources.what: Thierry et al. 2009, PNAS: Greek has two basic terms, ghalazio (light blue) and ble (dark blue); visual mismatch negativity to light versus dark blue was larger in Greek than in English speakers, with no group difference for green

items.notes: Subject: social science (linguistics, psychology). Key letter A. Cause in a Because clause in the blank’s sentence; key is evaluative (salient), distractors from the same family with the wrong ground. Steps: 2 (separate words, then stronger brain response, so the difference stands out). Corrected ranks: salient 21,092; inscrutable 10,108; ostentatious 20,698; innate 11,550; 4 of 4 past 10,000; mean log 4.18. Near miss: ostentatious (same field of conspicuousness, wrong agent and intent). Simplified: the green control is left out.

band7.why: Borderline: 4 of 4 options past 10,000 but only 2 past 20,000, mean log 4.18, rarest distractor 20,698; key salient (21,092) on a one-step cause clue, so the vocabulary carries it as in a756aa95; ostentatious is a near miss on agent and intent, innate reverses the cause.

items.passage: Precipitation and flooding remove roughly 22,000 tons of phosphorus, an essential plant nutrient, from Amazon soils each year. Hongbin Yu and colleagues estimate that dust transported from the Sahara replenishes approximately that quantity, so the rainforest is less ______ than its lushness suggests: its fertility depends partially on a desert across the Atlantic.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Insular means cut off and self-contained. The rainforest looks as though it sustains itself, but the phosphorus it loses is replaced by dust from the Sahara, so the forest depends on a distant desert and is less self-contained than it appears.

A.why_wrong: Precarious means unstable or at risk. A lush forest does not suggest precariousness to begin with, and the text says nothing about the forest being more secure than it looks.

C.why_wrong: Interdependent means relying on something else. That is what the finding shows, so the forest is more interdependent than it looks, not less.

D.why_wrong: Prolific means producing abundantly, which lushness does suggest. But the colon clause explains the blank by the forest’s reliance on a desert, not by any shortfall in how much it grows.

sources.what: ESSIC (University of Maryland) on Yu et al. 2015, Geophysical Research Letters: CALIPSO estimates of Saharan dust reaching the Amazon; about 22,000 tons of phosphorus a year, roughly the amount lost to rain and flooding

items.notes: Subject: natural science (earth science, ecology). Key letter B. Negated frame by comparative (“less ______ than its lushness suggests”), as in 2.14. Corrected ranks: precarious 13,764; insular 34,183; interdependent unseen; prolific 23,160.

items.passage: Beginning in 1968, New Zealand–born composer Annea Lockwood created Piano Transplants, a series of performances using irreparable instruments. She set one ablaze, submerged another, and partially buried others in a garden, leaving each piano ______ natural forces that would gradually transform both its structure and the sounds it produced.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To consign something to a force is to hand it over to that force’s control. Lockwood burned, sank, and buried the pianos and then let fire, water, and soil change them, so each instrument was handed over to natural forces.

A.why_wrong: Insulated from means protected from. Burning, sinking, and burying the pianos exposed them to natural forces rather than protecting them.

B.why_wrong: Composers are commissioned to write works, but natural forces cannot commission anything; Lockwood made the works herself.

D.why_wrong: Indebted to means owing something to. Nothing suggests the pianos owed anything to the forces that were changing them.

sources.what: ISSUE Project Room on Lockwood’s Piano Transplants (begun 1968): Piano Burning, Piano Garden and Piano Drowning, pianos beyond repair burned, planted in a garden and drowned

items.notes: Subject: humanities (music, sound art). Key letter C. Restatement by example (burned, sank, buried, then left to change). Corrected ranks: insulated from 48,468; commissioned by 1,580; consigned to 14,306; indebted to 11,122. Simplified: the drowning site is not named.

items.passage: Brazilian artist Mira Schendel produced her Monotipias in the mid-1960s by placing translucent Japanese rice paper over oiled glass and inscribing the reverse of each sheet with a fingernail or stylus. The resulting lines and characters appear ______: insubstantial and delicate, they seem to hover weightlessly across the almost transparent surface.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Ethereal means light and delicate, as if not quite of this world. The colon restates it: the marks are “insubstantial and delicate” and seem to “hover weightlessly” on paper one can almost see through.

B.why_wrong: Ponderous means heavy and slow. Marks that are insubstantial and seem to hover weightlessly are the opposite of heavy.

C.why_wrong: Methodical means orderly and systematic. The text describes how the lines look (insubstantial, floating), not an orderly pattern in them.

D.why_wrong: Derivative means copied from other work. Nothing compares the Monotipias with anyone else’s art.

sources.what: Hauser & Wirth, Mira Schendel: Monotypes: thin Japanese rice paper laid on oiled glass, drawn on from the back with fingernail or point; about 2,000 works in the mid-1960s

items.notes: Subject: humanities (art). Key letter A. Clue after the colon restates the key (faint, delicate, weightless). Corrected ranks: ethereal 12,604; ponderous 8,444; methodical 18,651; derivative 4,627.

items.subtype: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
items.passage: In 1783 Belinda Sutton, enslaved for decades by Isaac Royall Jr., petitioned the Massachusetts legislature for financial support from Royall’s estate, which the state had confiscated after he fled as a Loyalist. Because her uncompensated labor had helped ______ the estate’s considerable wealth, she argued, a portion of that wealth was rightfully hers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To amass is to gather or build up a large amount. Sutton’s claim to a share of the wealth rests on the idea that her unpaid work helped produce it, so her labor helped amass the estate’s wealth.

A.why_wrong: To squander is to waste. If her labor had wasted the wealth, it would give her no claim to a share of it; her argument depends on having helped create it.

B.why_wrong: To appraise is to estimate value. Her labor did not value the estate; it produced the wealth, which is why she claimed part of it.

C.why_wrong: To bequeath is to leave property by will, a word linked to estates. Only an owner can bequeath wealth; Sutton’s labor could not, and the text says her work helped create it.

sources.what: Royall House and Slave Quarters, Belinda Sutton and her petitions: 1783 petition to the Massachusetts General Court for support from the estate of Isaac Royall Jr., a Loyalist; wealth “accumulated by her own industry”; pension granted

items.notes: Subject: history. Key letter D. Cause clue: her claim to the wealth follows only if her labor built it. Corrected ranks: squander 27,047; appraise 33,970; bequeath 28,363; amass 38,783. The petition’s own phrase (“accumulated”) is not used in the passage, so the key paraphrases it.

fixes: "approximately five decades" changed to "decades": fifty years is the petition's own figure and historians put it nearer four

items.passage:
The following text is from O. E. Rølvaag’s 1924–1925 novel Giants in the Earth (translated by Lincoln Colcord and the author in 1927). Newly arrived Norwegian settlers are sitting together at dusk on the Dakota prairie.

The faces that gazed into one another were sober now, as silence <u>claimed</u> the little company; but lines of strength and determination on nearly every countenance told of an inward resolve to keep the mood of depression from gaining full control.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “claimed” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: The talk has stopped and the faces are “sober now”: silence has come over the group. In this sentence “claimed” means that silence took hold of the company, or overtook it, while the settlers resolve not to let the gloomy mood take full control.

A.why_wrong: People claim a right by demanding it, but silence is not asking the settlers for anything; it is settling over them.

C.why_wrong: To claim that something is true is to assert it, but silence makes no statement; the sentence describes the group falling quiet.

D.why_wrong: One claims lost property by recovering it, but nothing has been lost and taken back; the company simply becomes silent.

sources.what: Text of Giants in the Earth (A. L. Burt, 1927; translated by Lincoln Colcord), Project Gutenberg 75491; excerpt copied exactly from Book I

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter B. Abstract sense of a common verb (silence claimed the company), as in 2.19 (assumed greater precision). All three distractors are other senses of “claim” (a right, an assertion, lost property). Norwegian volumes I de dage (1924) and Riket grundlægges (1925); English edition 1927, public domain in the US. Excerpt copied exactly (one sentence).

items.passage: American woodworker Wharton Esherick ______ the line between furniture and sculpture. The red oak spiral staircase he handcrafted for his studio in Paoli, Pennsylvania, functions as an ordinary staircase, yet it is also celebrated as sculpture and was exhibited at the 1939 New York World’s Fair.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The staircase is both a working staircase and a sculpture shown at a world’s fair, so it is hard to say which side of the line between furniture and sculpture it belongs on. Esherick blurred that line.

A.why_wrong: Guarding the line would mean keeping furniture and sculpture clearly apart, but his staircase is both at once.

B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text is about giving the line a name; it describes an object that is both furniture and art.

D.why_wrong: To trace a line is to follow or outline it. Esherick’s staircase does not follow the boundary between furniture and sculpture; it belongs to both sides at once.

sources.what: Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia, Arts of Wharton Esherick: studio in Paoli; hand-cut red oak spiral staircase (about 1930), both functional and sculpture, shown at the 1939 New York World’s Fair

items.notes: Subject: humanities (craft, design). Key letter C. Restatement in the next sentence (working staircase yet sculpture). Corrected ranks (reviewer recount, measure calibrated to the band-7 report): guarded 1,257; named 246; blurred 9,530; traced 2,471; 0 of 4 past 10,000; mean log 3.22.

fixes: notes ranks named options not in the item; recounted for the printed options

items.passage: Biologist Mayako Kutsukake and colleagues study the aphid Nipponaphis monzeni, which forms colonies inside plant growths called galls. When a gall is punctured, juvenile soldier aphids rush to ______ it: they discharge enormous quantities of body fluid that solidifies over the opening like a scab.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The soldiers release fluid that hardens over the hole like a scab, which closes the opening in the gall. Sealing a tear in this way is repairing it.

B.why_wrong: To widen the gall’s opening would make the hole bigger, but the hardened fluid covers the hole and closes it.

C.why_wrong: The soldiers do more than visit the damaged spot: the text says they cover the hole with fluid that hardens like a scab.

D.why_wrong: The soldiers rush toward the damage and seal it; they do not leave the gall.

sources.what: Science News on Kutsukake et al. 2019, PNAS: soldier nymphs of Nipponaphis monzeni discharge large amounts of body fluid that clots and hardens into a scab to seal breaches in their gall

items.notes: Subject: natural science (entomology). Key letter A. Restatement after the colon. Corrected ranks (reviewer recount, measure calibrated to the band-7 report): repair 8,027; widen 22,285; visit 792; leave 302; 1 of 4 past 10,000; mean log 3.41.

fixes: notes ranks named options not in the item; recounted for the printed options

items.passage: For more than five decades, Ida Lewis helped maintain the Lime Rock Light, a lighthouse in the harbor of Newport, Rhode Island. She became famous for her ______: repeatedly she rowed into treacherous, frigid water to rescue people from overturned boats, and she is credited with saving at least eighteen lives.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The colon explains why Lewis became famous: she rowed again and again into “treacherous, frigid water” to rescue people. Facing that danger repeatedly shows bravery.

A.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns money; Lewis is famous for what she did on the water.

C.why_wrong: Rowing into treacherous, frigid water again and again is the opposite of avoiding risk, so caution is not what made her famous.

D.why_wrong: The text gives no sign that Lewis was known for being funny; it describes rescues.

sources.what: US Coast Guard history (Women in the Coast Guard): Ida Lewis, keeper of Lime Rock Light, Newport, credited with saving about 18 to 24 people by rowing out to capsized boats

items.notes: Subject: history. Key letter B. Restatement after the colon. Corrected ranks: wealth 1,459; bravery 10,077; caution 4,468; humor 3,201. Lewis lived at Lime Rock from 1857 to 1911.

items.passage:
The following text is from Nellie McClung’s 1908 novel Sowing Seeds in Danny. The novel is set in an agricultural community in Manitoba, Canada.

The creek, swollen with the July rain, <u>ran</u> full in its narrow channel, sparkling and swirling over its gravelly bed, and on the green meadow below the house a herd of shorthorns contentedly cropped the tender after-grass.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “ran” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: The subject of “ran” is a creek swollen with rain, moving “full in its narrow channel” and “swirling over its gravelly bed.” Water that runs in a channel flows.

A.why_wrong: A person can run a business by managing it, but a creek does not manage anything.

B.why_wrong: People run away when they flee, but the creek is not escaping from anything; it is moving along its channel.

C.why_wrong: A machine runs when it operates, but the text describes water moving over a gravelly bed, not a machine working.

sources.what: Text of Sowing Seeds in Danny (1908), Project Gutenberg 4376; sentence copied exactly from chapter VII

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter D. Concrete physical sense of a common verb, as in 1.56 and 1.4. All three distractors are other senses of “run.” Setting: Millford, a fictional Manitoba town.

items.passage:
The following text is from Barbara Baynton’s 1902 short story “A Dreamer.” A young woman, arriving unexpectedly, has reached her mother’s isolated house during a nighttime storm.

She was not daunted when the bark of the old dog brought no one to the door. It might not be heard inside, for there was such a torrent of water falling somewhere close. Mechanically her mind located it. The tank near the house, <u>fed</u> by the spouts was running over, cutting channels through the flower beds, and flooding the paths.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “fed” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: The tank is “fed by the spouts” and is “running over”: water from the spouts pours into it until it overflows. Here “fed” means supplied with water.

B.why_wrong: People and animals are fed in the sense of being nourished with food, but a water tank does not eat; the spouts send water into it.

C.why_wrong: Feelings can be fed in the sense of being encouraged, but the text is about water filling a tank, not about anything growing stronger in someone’s mind.

D.why_wrong: Feeding a hungry person satisfies them, but a tank has no hunger to satisfy; it is overflowing with water.

sources.what: Text of Bush Studies (1902), Project Gutenberg 78420; paragraph copied exactly from “A Dreamer”

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter A. Concrete sense of a common verb fixed by its frame (fed by the spouts, running over). Distractors are other senses of “feed.” The source has no comma after “spouts”; kept as printed.

items.passage:
The following text is from Duncan Campbell Scott’s 1896 short story “Josephine Labrosse.” Josephine and her mother have converted their front room into a small shop.

“Mother,” said Josephine, “we belong to the people who do not succeed.”

“True!” replied Madame Labrosse, disconsolately. “But we must live, and there is the mother,” and she <u>cast</u> her eyes to the corner where her own mother sat, drawing at her pipe, so dark and withered as to look like a piece of punk that had caught fire and was going off in smoke.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “cast” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Madame Labrosse mentions “the mother” and then looks toward the corner where her own mother sits. To cast one’s eyes somewhere is to turn one’s gaze there.

A.why_wrong: Metal is cast when it is poured into a mold, but Madame Labrosse is not shaping her eyes; she is looking toward her mother.

B.why_wrong: Animals cast off skin or feathers when they shed them, but nothing is being shed here; she simply looks at the corner.

D.why_wrong: A director casts an actor by selecting them, but Madame Labrosse is not choosing anything; she directs her gaze.

sources.what: Text of In the Village of Viger (1896), Project Gutenberg 48998; passage copied exactly from “Josephine Labrosse”

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter C. “Cast her eyes” fixes the sense; all three distractors are other senses of “cast.” Copied exactly (punk here means tinder).

items.passage: Lynd Ward’s 1929 book Gods’ Man narrates the story of an artist who trades his soul for a magical paintbrush entirely through wood engravings, without a single word of text. Because later artists who told extended stories in pictures learned from books like it, Gods’ Man is frequently regarded as ______ today’s graphic novels.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Gods’ Man came first, and later picture-story artists learned from books like it. A work that later forms grew out of is their ancestor, so Gods’ Man is regarded as an ancestor of graphic novels.

A.why_wrong: A rival competes with something at the same time. Gods’ Man was made long before today’s graphic novels and influenced them; nothing suggests competition.

C.why_wrong: An imitation copies something that already exists. Gods’ Man came first and later artists learned from it, so the copying, if any, ran the other way.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests that Gods’ Man criticizes graphic novels; the text says later artists learned from books like it.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Gods’ Man: 1929 wordless novel by Lynd Ward in wood engravings; an artist trades his soul for a magic paintbrush; a precursor of the graphic novel whose development it influenced

items.notes: Subject: humanities (literature, printmaking). Key letter B. Cause clue (later artists learned from it). Corrected ranks: a rival of 3,703; an ancestor of 6,348; an imitation of 6,636; a critic of 6,165.

items.passage: During and after World War I, the US government seized patents owned by German companies and licensed many of them to American firms. Economists Petra Moser and Alessandra Voena found that in the chemical fields where US firms gained ______ these German inventions, patenting by American inventors rose by about 20 percent.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The government licensed the seized German patents to American firms, which let those firms use the inventions. Being allowed to use something is gaining access to it.

A.why_wrong: The firms were licensed to use the German inventions; the text does not say the inventions began competing with them.

B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text mentions complaints; it describes firms being licensed to use the patents.

C.why_wrong: Gaining distance from the inventions would mean moving away from them, but the licenses gave the firms the right to use them.

sources.what: Moser and Voena, “Compulsory Licensing: Evidence from the Trading with the Enemy Act” (NBER w15598; American Economic Review 2012): licensing of German-owned patents to US firms increased domestic invention in affected chemical fields by about 20 percent

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics, history of technology). Key letter D. Restatement of “licensed many of them to American firms.” Corrected ranks: competition from 2,613; complaints about 5,990; distance from 774; access to 1,622.

items.passage: California ground squirrels sometimes chew the shed skins of rattlesnakes and then lick their own fur. Because rattlesnakes rely heavily on smell to find prey, biologist Barbara Clucas and colleagues suggest that coating their fur with snake scent may help the squirrels ______ their own odor and avoid becoming a meal.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Rattlesnakes find prey by smell, and the squirrels cover their fur with snake scent. Covering their own smell with another one would make it harder for snakes to notice them, so the scent may help them disguise their odor.

A.why_wrong: If the squirrels made their own odor stronger, snakes that hunt by smell would find them more easily, not less.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the squirrels give their odor to anything else; they cover themselves with the snakes’ scent.

D.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the squirrels measure anything; the point is to keep snakes from smelling them.

sources.what: Clucas, Owings and Rowe 2008, Proceedings of the Royal Society B (PMC): California ground squirrels chew shed rattlesnake skin and lick their fur; the applied scent probably masks their own odor

items.notes: Subject: natural science (animal behavior). Key letter C. Cause clue (snakes hunt by smell). Hedged as the source is (“suggest … may help”). Corrected ranks: strengthen 2,132; share 980; disguise 4,211; measure 1,295.

items.passage: In 1908 mountaineer Annie Smith Peck reached the northern summit of Peru’s Huascarán and estimated its elevation at approximately 24,000 feet, enough to surpass Fanny Bullock Workman’s altitude record for women. Doubting that figure, Workman hired a team of French surveyors to ______ the peak; they determined it was only about 21,800 feet high.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Workman doubted Peck’s estimate of the mountain’s height, and the surveyors then reported how high the peak really was. Checking a height means measuring it.

B.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the surveyors gave the mountain a new name; they reported its height.

C.why_wrong: Workman doubted the figure that threatened her record, so she had no reason to pay people to honor the peak, and the surveyors’ job was to find its height.

D.why_wrong: The surveyors could not report the peak’s height by staying away from it; Workman paid them to study it.

sources.what: American Alpine Club Library, Annie Smith Peck and Fanny Bullock Workman: Peck’s 1908 ascent of Huascarán’s north peak, estimated at 24,000 feet; Workman hired French surveyors in 1909 who measured it at 21,812 feet

items.notes: Subject: history. Key letter A. Consequence clue (the surveyors found its height). Corrected ranks (reviewer recount, measure calibrated to the band-7 report): measure 350; rename unseen; honor 1,399; avoid 1,296; 1 of 4 past 10,000; mean log 3.70.

fixes: notes ranks named options not in the item; recounted for the printed options

items.passage: Ceramicist George Ohr of Biloxi, Mississippi, was renowned for the ______ shapes of his vessels. After throwing each vessel with remarkably thin walls, he would frequently twist, pinch, fold, or dent the still-pliable clay, ensuring that no two of his ceramic creations appeared identical.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The second sentence gives the examples: Ohr twisted, pinched, folded, and dented his pots, and no two appeared identical. Shapes made that way are irregular.

A.why_wrong: Balanced shapes are even and symmetrical, but twisting and denting the clay makes them uneven.

B.why_wrong: The text describes how the pots look, not whether they are useful.

C.why_wrong: Nothing suggests Ohr copied his shapes from others; no two of his own pieces even looked alike.

sources.what: Mississippi History Now, George E. Ohr: America’s First Art Potter: thin walls thrown on the wheel, then dented, ruffled, twisted and folded; no two alike

items.notes: Subject: humanities (ceramics). Key letter D. Example-pinned: the list of actions instantiates irregular. Corrected ranks (reviewer recount, measure calibrated to the band-7 report): balanced 727; practical 2,044; borrowed 2,132; irregular 5,683; 0 of 4 past 10,000; mean log 3.31.

fixes: "crumple" changed to "dent" (the source lists twisting, denting, ruffling and folding)

items.passage: The marsh periwinkle, a snail inhabiting salt marshes along North America’s Atlantic coast, cuts long wounds into the leaves of cordgrass. Ecologists Brian Silliman and Steven Newell discovered that the snails do this not mainly to ______ the grass: fungi colonize the wounds, and the snails subsequently consume the fungi.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The colon explains the snails’ real purpose: fungi colonize the wounds, and the snails then consume the fungi. So the snails cut the grass mainly to grow food, not to eat the grass itself.

A.why_wrong: Nothing suggests the snails press the grass down; they cut wounds into its leaves.

C.why_wrong: Wounding leaves and letting fungi grow in them harms the grass rather than protecting it, so “not to protect” would not be the point the colon explains.

D.why_wrong: Pollinating is something done for plants, but snails cutting wounds are not carrying pollen, and the colon is about what the snails eat.

sources.what: Silliman and Newell 2003, PNAS, “Fungal farming in a snail”: Littoraria irrorata grazes live marsh grass primarily not to feed but to prepare substrate for fungal growth, then eats the fungi

items.notes: Subject: natural science (ecology). Key letter B. Negated frame (“not mainly to ______”), as in 1.48. Corrected ranks (reviewer recount, measure calibrated to the band-7 report): flatten 40,388; eat 1,085; protect 1,157; pollinate unseen; 2 of 4 past 10,000; mean log 4.18.

fixes: "mainly not to ______" reordered to "not mainly to ______" (standard placement of the negator)

items.passage:
The following text is from May Sinclair’s 1919 novel Mary Olivier: A Life. The narrator describes customary evening gatherings at the Olivier household, where relatives and neighbors frequently visited.

At half-past eight Catty would bring in the tea-tray; the white and grey and gold tea-cups would be <u>set out</u> round the bulging silver tea-pot that lifted up its spout with a foolish, pompous expression, like a hen. Mamma would move about the table in her mauve silk gown, and there would be a scent of cream and strong tea.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the phrase “set out” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Catty brings in the tea-tray, and the cups are placed in a ring “round the bulging silver tea-pot.” Cups that are set out around a teapot are arranged there.

A.why_wrong: A writer sets out an argument by explaining it, but tea-cups are objects being placed on a table, not ideas being explained.

B.why_wrong: Travelers set out when they depart on a journey, but the cups are not going anywhere; they are put around the teapot.

D.why_wrong: Gardeners set out seedlings by planting them, but cups on a tea-tray are not planted in soil.

sources.what: Text of Mary Olivier: A Life (1919), Project Gutenberg 9366; passage copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter C. Phrase target with all three distractors other senses of “set out” (an argument, a journey, seedlings). Copied exactly from Book III.
